stops.name: Tours, the armor and the standard
stops.campa: At Tours, in Yolande's own Angevin territory, the white armor is fitted to the Maid's measure and the painter works her standard of lilies and the names of God. Yolande's household absorbs the girl into its own machinery of war-making, the same machinery that has clothed and armed Angevin captains for a generation, so that by the time Jehanne rides north she carries not only her voices but the full material weight of a duchy's treasury behind her, spent by a woman who has been financing armies since before the girl from Domrémy was born.

stops.name: Blois, the convoy funded; the army blessed
stops.campa: At Blois the relief convoy for Orléans musters: carts of grain, droves of cattle, captains and men-at-arms, funded in substantial part out of Yolande's own resources, her dower lands and her long-managed treasury of Anjou and Provence, at a moment when the royal exchequer itself can barely pay its clerks. She has, in effect, underwritten the turn of the Hundred Years' War with her own household's money, betting a duchess's fortune on a peasant girl's voices because the alternative, La Trémoille's endless caution, has already cost the kingdom Orléans nearly seven months.

stops.name: Angers, the letter from Reims, the coronation by proxy
stops.campa: Yolande is not at Reims. While the Sainte Ampoule is carried into the cathedral and Charles is anointed with the oil of Clovis, she waits at Angers for word, as she has waited through every campaign of her life's great project. It comes in a letter from three gentlemen of Anjou in the coronation train, addressed jointly to Queens Marie and Yolande, mother and daughter, wife and mother-in-law, the two women whose sixteen years of marriage-brokering and financing have just been crowned in a cathedral neither of them was permitted, by the danger of the roads, to enter.

stops.name: Angers, the son a duke, then a prisoner
stops.campa: Word reaches Yolande of a double reversal in her son René's fortune: heir to Bar since 1419 and sole duke since Cardinal Louis's death the year before, he has now succeeded also to Lorraine on his father-in-law's death, only to be met at Bulgneville by the rival claimant Antoine de Vaudemont and a Burgundian relief force. René is defeated and taken prisoner. Yolande, who has spent her whole life converting marriages into territory, watches one of her own conversions collapse into a cell; René will not come home for years.

stops.name: Chinon, La Trémoille seized in his chamber
stops.campa: At Chinon, where the Maid first found her king, Yolande's own faction closes on the favorite who has held Charles's ear and thwarted her policy for six years. Conspirators, Richemont, her son Charles of Anjou, Pierre de Brézé and others acting with Yolande's sanction, force their way into Georges de La Trémoille's chamber by night; a dagger-thrust meant to kill him is turned aside by his own great fat, and he is dragged off instead to captivity and ransom. No new favorite replaces him. In his place stand, plainly now, the two Angevin queens.

stops.name: Angers and Saumur, the court reordered around the two queens
stops.campa: With La Trémoille broken, the government Charles VII actually keeps is, for the rest of the 1430s, Yolande's own: her son Charles of Anjou at the council table, Richemont commanding in the field, Pierre de Brézé rising through her patronage, and she herself moving between Angers and Saumur, writing the letters and brokering the truces no chronicle credits to a woman's hand at the time but every later historian traces back to her drawing room. She has stopped needing to be present at the great events; by now the great events are simply staffed by her people.

stops.name: Saumur, Margaret of Anjou raised
stops.campa: At Saumur, Yolande takes her granddaughter Margaret, René's daughter, not yet ten, into her own household, teaching her the accounts, the etiquette and the literature of the same curriculum that once shaped Marie for the throne of France. She is grooming the girl, without yet saying so, for the English match that will one day make her Queen of England and the fiercest Lancastrian of the Wars of the Roses. Louis XI, decades later, will say of the grandmother what could as easily be said of the whole design: that she carried a man's heart in a woman's body.

stops.name: Saumur, the retreat, the court's turn away
stops.campa: In her last years the court she built begins, in small ways, to outgrow her. Charles VII, secure now on a throne she spent thirty years securing for him, listens increasingly to younger men who owe her nothing; the Praguerie revolt of 1440, in which her own son-in-law's rivals briefly rise against the king, is a reminder that the peace she engineered was never permanent. Yolande withdraws more and more to Saumur, old, still writing letters, still arranging marriages, no longer at the center of every decision she once made alone.

stops.name: Saumur, death at the house of Tucé
stops.campa: Yolande dies at Saumur, in the town house of the Seigneur de Tucé, on the fourteenth of November, sixty-one years old. She has outlived a father, a husband, a rival queen, and very nearly the kingdom itself, and has spent every year of her widowhood turning a disinherited boy into an anointed king. She dies without ever having worn a crown that was fully, legally her own: Aragon lost at Caspe, Naples never held, Sicily and Jerusalem only titles; the one kingdom she actually built, France, crowned in a country she made and did not rule.

stops.name: Angers, burial in the cathedral of Saint-Maurice
stops.campa: Her body is carried to Angers and laid in the cathedral of Saint-Maurice, in the city she chose over every capital her four kingdoms could have offered her. Charles VII, the boy she refused to send back to his own mother, is by now unmistakably the king she promised the Bois Chenu prophecy would make of him; Marie, her daughter, is his queen; Richemont, her appointment, is his constable. The tapestry Yolande wove for thirty years is, at her death, simply called France, and no one troubles any longer to name the weaver.

stops.name: Aix-en-Provence, coda: René, the Good King, the troubadour-king
stops.campa: Her second son René, ransomed at last from Burgundian captivity, briefly King of Naples, permanently Duke of Bar and titular king of a half-dozen realms he never rules by force, settles in his last decades at Aix, the same comital court where his mother once kept troubadours between two languages of statecraft. He paints, gardens, writes allegories of love and death, holds tournaments by his own devised rules, and becomes to later ages the Good King René of Provençal legend, the courtly and occult-tinged afterlife of the house Yolande built, still carrying, through him, the county of Bar back toward the ground of Domrémy.
